WASHINGTON. Jan. 3.-The following
weather-crop bulletin has been issued by
the Department of Agriculture:


While the deficiency in temperature for
the month was greatest in the Northwest,
the cold was relatively more severe through
out the Southern States A cold wave ex-
tended southwark. causing killing frosts as
far south as Jupiter. Fla, and along the
Gulf coast ON the 29th, and for several days
the temperature was from 10 to 20 degrees
below freezing over the greater portion of
the Southern States Excessive rains oc-
CURED in the Lower Mississippi Valley aud
generally over the regions south Of the Mis-
souri, and north of tie Rio Grande Valley.
In the month it was generally dry through
out the regions on the Atlantic Coast and
over the Ohio Valley ana lake region. On
the Pacific Coast, while the rainfall was
generally less than usual, 1t was timely and
sufficient in quantity to prove of benefit
to the farmers. The month closed with the
ground covered with snow from New York
and the Upper Ohio Valley westward to
the Rocky Mountains and the ground bare
over the greater portion of Missouri, Hi
nois and Indiana and thence southwark.
thus leaving over half the winter wheat
without the protection afforded by the
snow.

NEW YORK, Sept. THE first OF the
series of trial races to determine which of
the new American sloops is best fitted 10
compete with the English yacht Valkyrie
in the coming international races for the
possession cf the America cup was held
to-day. The course was from Scotland
Lightship to and around a float fifteen
miles to windward ami return, flushing at
the starting point. The competing yachts
were the Viglant, Jubilee and Coionia,
the Pilgrim having Withdrawn from the
race because of a broken gaff. The Colo
MIA won the race, with the Vigilant six


econds behind.


A twenty-mle breeze was blowing from
the southeast as the yachts started aud the
sea was moderately rough. Before start
ing the ColoDia had taken down her club
topsail and substituted one of ordinary
style. The Vigilant looked stumpy with
her topmast down, but she travelled like
Tam o. Shanter. Five minutes after the
start the Jubilee swung slowly around and
started back for New York like crippled
pigeon. She had broken the outer block
OF her gaff and withdrew. This left the
C ntest between the two Herreshoff boats.
and it Is evident the wind and weather
was too much for the Boston sloop.


The Vigilant and Colonia were now
standing of on different tacks, but both
were pointing almost in the eye of the
wind and were drawing it as fine as tbey
knew how. Both boats sailed indepen-
IDENTIFY and tackled where they liked, but the
conditions were absolutely the same. All
sailing craft were left far asiern, except
the pilot-boat Gerry. which hung like a
swift hawk on the flank of the racers.
Finally the race became monotony of
tacks, and it was apparent that the Vigil
ant had brrrowed her way up into the
wind. leaving the Colonia quarter of a
mile aftern.


The stakeboat was finally sighted. and
this was where the interest in the race
reached its greatest height. The Vigiiant
bad set her 'opmast and tops IN some time
before standing for The buoy, aud Just be-
fore reaching it the Vigilant threw her
long spnnaker boom to port, followed
few moments later by the Cnlonia. Shaw
Ing the red flag by a few feet the ViCliant
squared away for home and brought out
her great spl maker few moments after
rounding. The Colonia was about five
minutes behind. but she gained gradually
on the Vigilant in the home run. Inch by
inch and foot by foot she crelt up, and
when the finish gun was fired she had won
By six seconds.

The great anti-Semitic meeting was held at
the Tivoli-vauxhall, Paris last evening, under

proval. The principal speaker of the evening

French honor.

tions, and about fifty men started forward to
dispute with the marquis his place on the plat
form. At the steps of the platform they met
some thirty partisans of the Libre Parole
group, who showed fight. Police Commissioner
Neron announced that unless the disorder
ceased he must dissolve the meeting and a
short lull followed.

Hebrews. with the declaration that were it not
for them and other capitalists like them the
social question would be solved easily

state of affairs which was eliminating in the
Panama scandal They rejoiced in such ruin of

proceed.

break, could not be heard by those almost

way. Commissary Veron then called in two

SANTA BARBARA, July 17.-Vice- Presi-
dent Stevenson and party arrived tonight
about half-past o'clock on the steamer
Corona from San Diego. They were driven
directly to the Franciscan mission, which
the visitors had expressed desire to see.


The guests were received by the padres,
who showed them through the church,
decorated for the occasion. After few
moments they again entered carriages and
were taken TO the San Marcos, where a
reception was given.


Notwithstanding the lateness of the
hour, quite large crowd had gathered at
the hotel to witness the reception of the
Vice-President. The reception-room was
brilliantly lighted and decorated and was
packed when the guests were escorted 10
an address of welcome.


General Stevenson replied, expressing
thanks for the cordialiry which had been
shown 70 himself and others on the trip
through the Golden State.


Mrs. Stevenson was presented with an
album containing about twenty-five views
of the Channel City and vicinity.


Other members of the party besides the
Vice. President spoke, but the guests de.
parted for the boat, already four hours
late. before large number of Barbarenos
who were present were presented to Mr..
Stevenson.


The Corona sailed about midnight with
the stinguished passengers on her way
north. From San Diego up she had very
nice trip and the visitors seem to be
greatly enjoying the voyage.

Walter Eytinge, leading man in the
"Span of Life" Company, now playing at

The deceased actor joined the company

now his widow, early last evening.

hours later the wires carried second

lean inland and tfemble at the cry of thirst

rebellion for the sea-


1t is only when the sun lowers it's p.oad

mouths for the moist kiss of night; only
when the silver sand has slaked it's thirst,

never ending combat they play again their

Yesterday afternoon an inquest was held at
the sixth police precinct over the body of
Armistead Nickings, the colored man whose
legs were cut off Monday last by an engine on
the Baltimore and Potomac railroad at LIST
street and Virginia avenue southwest. The
testimony Of several bystanders and railroad
people was heard, and the jury after few mo-
ments' elaboration rendered verdict to the
effect that the man came to his death through
his own carelessness and held the railroad
blameless in the matter. 1t appeared from the
evidence that the unfortunate man in passing
down LIST street found train Of empty passen-
ger cars standing at the crossing. and being in
. hurry to get past Armistead, despite the gate
mans warning, passed under the lowered gates,
jumped upon one Of the cars and then jumped
on the opposite track. almost directly in front
Of passing engine. The engine was running
slowly, and only the first wheel passed over the
man.

The New York Tribune says: The Nicaragua
Canal Construction Company Is out Of funds
and has stopped all work upon the Nicaragua
canal. For some time It has been rumored
thatthe company has been affected by the gen.
eral stringency in the money market, and it
has also become known that there are some
international dissensions In the Company and
that there has been great disappointment that
the management has failed to obtain loans from
this country and from England.


Yesterday the officers admitted that work
on the canal had been stopped. They said that
the failure to 60 ahead with the work was due
simply and solely to failure to raise money,
and they had not much doubt that when affairs
became easier the work would 60 on. For the
present, however, their vast plant in Central
America would remain idle


1t had been intimated that the stoppage of
construction had been due partly to the
political troubles and revolutions in Central
America. Those changes would, however,
have caused comparatively little trouble to the
company had it been supplied with funds to go
ahead with the work.

BRussELs, April 15.-The most serious dis
turbance that has yet occurred during the
present agitation against the chamber Of depu-
ties for rejecting the universal suffrage bill
took place last night at Joliment.


In q fight between the strikers and the gen.
darmes one woman was killed and three Of the
strikers seriously wounded. The strikers had
been acting desperately all dav and at night
began to assemble in great numbers. The
gendarmes attempted to disterse them and
met with strong resistance. In the mob OF
rioters were a number of women. who with
shrill voices and flashing eyes, encouraged the
men to give battle TO the police. Spurred on
by these women, the strikers fought desper-
ately when the gendarmes attempted to drive
them from the streets


Clubs and stones were freely used and there
was prospect of the mob getting the upper
hand of the gendarmes when the order
was given for the latter to draw their
swords and charge the crowd The order
was at once obeyed and slashing right and
left the gendarmes moved through the mob,
which broke and scattered in every direction,
hurting stones and any other handy missile
before they ran.


After the rioters were dispersed it was found
that one of the women had been hit with
sword and killed and that three men had been
SO badly wounded that they could not get away
from where they had fallen. The wounded
were removed to a hospital nd the body of the
woman to a morgue.


Further TROUBLE EXPECTED


The affair has caused great excitement and
further trouble is apprehended. The labor
leaders, many of whom are socialists, are striv-
ing in every way to make the strike
general. In Client their efforts are meet
ing with success and every day fresh
aecfn txf FL,
alton is acute, but the government is vIgilant.
The strikers in Client causing great excite
ment in that town Among the men who have
quit work are a large number of weavers. The
more orderly persons engaged in that occupa-
tion refused to join tine strikers, and the fact
greatly incensed the strikers


CLIENT RIOTERS ATTACK THE WORKING wEAvKRs.


Today the latter determined to force the
working weavers to leave their looms, and in
consequence a bloody riot ensued. The riot
ers. numbering hundreds. attacked the workers
and severely injured many of them. The po-
lice were promptly at the scene, but they were
powerless to handle the mob.


The strikers, aided by the usual crowd of
loafers and vagabonds, turned the police,
and though tine latter had the advantage of
being armed they were put to rout The police
by the stones fired at them.


The entire portion Of the city in which the
disturbance occurred was in an uproar. The
strikers. after the retreat of the police, took
possession of the quarter and acted in a most
disgraceful manner.


THE MILITARY CALLED OUT.


The civil authorities finding that the riot was
growing worse every minute called upon the
military for aid. Under orders from the CEN
trail authorities, which appears to realize the
gravity Of the movement, the troops were
ready to render assistance whenever called
upon.


A detachment Of cavalry was ordered to dis
perse the mob. They at once proceeded to the
scene of the rioting, and upon the order to dis
perse being greeted with derisive yells
they charged the mob. The latter
fed precipitately when they saw the
cavalrymen riding with drawn swords upon
them and sought refuge in houses and alley
ways. Not all escaped, however. Some of the
less fleet OF foot were knocked down and
trampled upon by the horses. while others were
struck by swords and badly hurt

at Mayfield.


MAYFIELD, KY, May Bob Brown, the
negro murderer, was hanged at 10:46 this morn
ing The body was cut down at minutes pas
II o'clock.


Browns CRIME.


The crime for which Brown suffered the
death penalty was the murder Of Albert Colley,
a well-to-do farmer Of this county. During his
career Brown had shot two white and three
colored men. He was twenty-seven years old
and has played the role of a desperate ever
since he located in this place, two years ago


He confessed being the person who stoned
Policeman Ezells residence about six months
ago, and declared his intention was to kill the
officer when he made his appearance at the door,
but fortunately Ezell was absent from home
at the time. The shooting Of Farmer Colley
occurred on the night of December 10, 1892,
at the houSe Of Polly Handy, notorious
white woman, where they met The woman
was Browns paramour and he objected to
Colley's presence.


A fight ensued in which Brown, together with
Dave Sheriff., another negro tough, and the
Handy woman forced Colley out of the house
into the back yard, where Brown brutally shot
him down. The two negroes were arrested and
Jailed, but the woman made her escape She
was subsequently arrested and brought back by
detectives.


The men we're tried at the April term Of
court and Brown was condemned to hang while
Sheriff. was given life sentence. The woman
will be tried at the next term Of court.

The United States cruiser Detroit, built by
the Columbian Iron Works and Dry Dock Com
pany Of Baltimore, made her Official four-hour
run yesterday. The speed made by the new
vessel was 49, 4s knots per hour. This remarka-
BILE speed astonished all on board except her
builders. Many who have seen the vessel under
way believed the severity of the official trial
would reduce her speed. The steamer sus-
tanned the trial gracefully and kept up a regu-
lar speed throughout without serious accident
to mar her progress or prevent her from dis
tinguishing herself. After suffering so much
disappointment. occasioned by unfavorable
weather, not q few were inclined to deal in
superstitious thought that the vessel was ILL.,
fated, but, instead of such discouraging result,
the product of Baltimore mechanics came out
OF the race pride to all connected with her
construction.


Since Wednesday last, after the preliminary
trial In Newport harbor. the Detroit has been
awaiting weather preparations for her final run
and yesterday turned out to be all that could be
wished for. either by the contractors or the
naval officials. At ten minutes past 8 o'clock
Admiral Belknap and the members of the naval
board left New London, Conn. and Joined the
cruiser in the harbor, and twenty minutes after
that she was on her way down the Thames
river. passing out of the river at the New Lon
don light. At $40 the vessel was run d0wn the
sound at not more than ten knots. and reached
the starting point off Plum Island shortly after
10 O'Clock, but as high water did not take place
till 1888 the cruiser was compelled to wait
nearly an hour.


GREAT TEST BEGUN.


At rs the Detroit Strengthened out about
two miles from the starting range and ran
down twice like horse before she got
under way as best she could. When she came
down for the third time every piece Of her con-
struction trembled as il with determination.
No one was on the forward deck but the naval
officers and constructors, the others aboard
stood on the deck. A glance at the countenances
of the little assembly showed their excitement
The wind made by the cruisers majestic strides
through the water made it any thing but pleas
ant to remain on deck. but all suffered this to
witness the vessels performance.


As she passed the starting range forty-fve
minutes eighteen seconds past II the signal bell
was sounded ana the excitement aboard was in
tense. Every one stood with his watch in hand
breathlessly watching every motion of the YES
sci. In the bow Admiral Belknap and Presi-
dent Master stood side by side. while Com
mander Brownson. the commander OF the new
vessel, paced the bridge. The countenances of
all glowed with satisfaction.


THE TIDE AGAINST HER.


The tide on the run down was unfavorable
for the vessels best work, but little effect was
noticeable in the resistance. At fourteen min
utes and thirty seconds past IL the steamer
passed the first nine-miie boat, which marked
the first quarter of the run.


This distance was covered in twenty-nine
minutes twelve seconds. This run was the best
made in the first half OF the whole run. but on
the return the great squirt made on the first
quarter, the Detroit having run the nine miles
In twenty-six minutes and eight seconds. which
is equal TO nearly nineteen knots per hour. The
entire running time of the cruiser three
hours. tfty-four minutes and twelve seconds.
bringing the steamer over the finish line six
minutes and twelve seconds before the allowed
time by the Navy Department for the run.


The time consumed in making the trial shows
the Detroit's speed to be at least a knot and
one-haf better than the specifications ask for


PREMIUM OF $4,000.


For this excess of speed the builders will re-
ceive S150.000. the highest premium ever paid
to any shipbuilder by the United States gov
eminent. The figures showing the speed made
by the Detroit were taken by the press repre-
sentatives and confirmed by the naval officers.
The official records will not be made public
until the observations are obtained from the
coast survey steamers Bache and Blake, which
were respectively stationed nine miles from the
start and nine miles from the finish of the
course. These have taken the speed Of the
tide when the cruiser was running both with
and against ii and as the tide was running it is
very probable an allowance will be made in
favor of the Detroit, which may give her an
official record of about lS$4 knots


Deductions may also be taken for the tide
running with the steamer ON her run up the
course, which would decrease her speed record.
This, however, naval officers state is not prob
able. The average mile made on the run was

How Capt. Scott's Daughters Cheered Up


the Crew OF the Hyderabad.


From the San Francisco Report


The British ship Hyderabad arrived this
morning from Swansea after a most eventful
voyage OF 272 days. CAPT. d. F. B. Scott has
his two daughters with him. and both the young
ladies assert that they never want to make a
similar trip. This is the Hyderabad's maiden
attempt, and Capt. Scott hopes he will never
have q similar experience while he remains
skipper of her.


After being launched and fitted out, the Hy-
derabad was loaded with coal at Swansea and
started for San Francisco. All went well until
September 9, when the ship ran into storm
The stanchlons gave way, boats were smashed.
the galley was washed overheard, the cabin
was flooded, and finally the cargo shifted.
While the ship was lying on her beam ends the
foretopgallant mast went by the board and it
looked as though the ship was doomed


1t was regular Cape Horn weather. and the
men were almost dead from cold. In spite Of
the fact that death was imminent, the captain 8
daughters were not dismsyed. They made
coffee over tho coal oil stove in the cabin and
served it to the half-frozen men whenever an
opportunity occurred. The men assert that
many times the young women made their way
forward when ladders, pieces of boats and hen
coops were all awash.


Inc gale lasted nearly week, and then con-
trary winds were met Capt. Scott was about
to give up in despair and start for San Fran
cisco via the Cape Of Good Hope. when on
October II it came on to blow again. All the
temporary yards were blown away and almost
entire suit Of sails was lost. The weight of
water that came laundering on board bent the
deck beams and the vessel began to leak. The
cargo shifted again and everybody prepared for
the worst. A conference of the officers was
held in the cabin and it was decided to make
for the Falkland Islands. The men were ex-
hausted by this time and refused to work.
Many OF them were sick and did not care
whether they lived or died. The captain 8
daughters went among them, bound up their
wounds, and. with steaIning hot coffee. into
which the captain put ''stick'' on the sly,
persuaded the men to return TO duty. Five
days later Port Stanley was reached. and for
the time the trouble was over. 1t took 100 days
to repair the ship, and then another start was
made.

The Illinois Centrars Chicago and New

tracked and ditched at Lime Switch, two
miles north of Ullin, ILL.,, at 1 O'Clock yester-
day morning, and Fireman Charles Ham
mond of Certralia instantly killed


There is every reason to believe that the
work was one of train wreckers, as the
switch track runs out to a lime kiln, and is
never used by passenger trains The lock
was broken, the switch was turned and the
lantern thrown into ditch


The train was behind time and running at
a high rate of speed and was some distance
out on the side switch before the engineer
discovered that anything was wrong The
track gave way under the ponderous engine
and the tender was overturned burying the
fireman beneath the ruins. The baggage
and express car followed, rolled over on its
side imprisoning the express messenger and
two guards within it, but without serious
injury.


Three coaches left the track, but did not
turn over and none of the passengers were
injured. There were ten vestibuled coaches
in the train, besides President Fish's pri-
vate car which was occupied by Mr.. Fish
and his private secretary. The train was
DELAYED until another engine could be sent
from Cairo to bring down the coaches that
had remained on the rails.

Steward William c. Holman of the whaling
schooner Leon s. Swift Of New Bedford Mass,
has reported the loss Of the schooner at the
Island of Mayo, Cape Verde Islands, February
10. The first mate. Edgar Grape Of New Bed
ford, the second mate and nine men were lost
The schooner had been away from her home
port since November IA. 1892, and has had poor
luck. In running down between Mayo and
Santiago in fog one night the vessel struck
the breakers on Former Island. boat was
lowered and five men and Mate Grape jumped
in. They had not gone two boat lengths from
the schooner when breaker capsized it, and
a moment later the second boat with four
men. also caps,zed. All were drowned.


The Swift was pounded in-shore and the
waves dashed over her ten feet high. When
she had brought up, wedged in between two
big boulders, the crew cut away her masts and
using them as bridges crawled ashore. The
crew saved nothing excepting what they had
on. They were taken to the American consul
at Port Praya. and were cared for. The Swift
was owned by P. H. Mye and others Of New Bed
ford, and valued at SIT 900; partially insured.

PORTLAND, Jan. 15.-A wood train on the
Portland & Willamette Valley railroad,
narrow gauge. met with a serious accident
this afternoon near Oswego, twelve miles
south OF this city, which resulted in the in
jury of sixteen persons. Every one on board
except Conductor Kennedy and Engineer
Miller was hurt, several seriously and
two probably fatally. The train con-
sisted of the engine and caboose
and twenty-four fat cars. Seven dat
cars were between the locomotive
and the caboose and the remainder
behind. There were seventeen men in the
caboose. While going round a curve and
approaching a trestle the engineer saw
large tree across the track, but realized
that he could not stop in time, so he
shut off steam and jumped. The
conductor, who was on the engine, fol-
lowed him. The engine struck the tree,
and was thrown from the track, falling
about fifteen feet off the trestle. Seven
fat cars and the caboose also went of, the
latter being badly smashed.


All the passengers were shaken up more
or less, and Raphael Cowtze was probably
fatally injured. Fireman John Hoben-
leitner was caught under the engine and
scalded. He also received internal in
juries and may die.

'The little town Of Camden, Me-. ought to
have its name changed to Hope" said dealer
in ship supplies and stores to New York Sun
man. 'for it turns out more Of the emblems of
hope than all the other places in this country
combined. All Of the stately ships that come
out of the Maine shipyards look to that little
village on the Penobscot for their anchors.
Scores Of sturdy smiths swing their hammers
day after day all the year long in the black,
smoky, long, low Camden shops, where only
anchors are forged. Sometimes the tripham-
mers are going all night about the FORCES, and
the blazing OF the fires and the ring of the
hammers are seen and heard miles away.
Thousands Of tons of old iron acs purchased by
these queer establishments every year, for an
chors are forged largely from cast-off iron. The
material is cut into email pieces by great shears
that clip through the iron as easily as a
cheese knife slices a cheese The pieces are
bound into bundles by strong wires, and are
then fused in the FORCES. Then they are
pounded and welded into the various parts
OF the anchor. some workmen fashioning the
rings, others shaping the fukes. others ham,
mering out the palms and others forging the
shanks. Then the complesers take the differ
ent parts and fuse and weld them into the fin
ished anchor. Anchors Of all sizes aud weights
are turned out from the noisy shops Of Cam
den, the graceful little pleasure boat anchor,
weighing but few pounds, as well rs the great
50 900 and u, 900 pound anchors Of tine biggest
ships.


There are many interesting relics at Cam
den in the line Of rusty and broken anchors
that did duty in their day on famous merchant
vessels, historic war ships and sturdy whalers.
Whatis left OF the anchor of the United States
frigate Cumberland is among these relics"

State of Washington followed five minutes
later and passed the Fleetwood soon after
rounding Robinson's point. Neither

that time, but they immediately fired up
for race. Pulley point was passed at
Alb, the State leading by length. In the
course OF fifteen minutes the Fleetwood
passed her and left her some lengths
astern.


Just before Alki point was reached the
State commenced to come ahead. The
Fleetwood people had trouble with their
wood, it being damp and too large. so the
passengers turned in with axes and split
it for the tiremen.

again passed the Fleetwood and crossed
her bows. Soon after her steam gave out

The trial of James Hards for . murder
committed twenty-five years ago was con-
Guided last night Dand the jury this morn
ing brought in verdict of manslaughter.


Twenty-Five years ago Hards was en-

left . few years later married Charles
Thurman, with whom she lived happily
until his death. A year ago she was called

yet been sentenced.

The Equipment.


They decided to start from Fort Smith on
the border of the Indian territory. and early
in the month of September the long jour
ney was begun with an ordinary farm
wagon and trusty team Of horses. The
wagon was covered with heavy ducking,


thick enough to turn the average western
rain. Cooking utensils and a supply Of
provisions sufficient until Guthrie was
reached and a sufficiency Of bedding were
packed into the deep wagon box like sar-
dimes.


The first one hundred miles lay through
the beautiful Cherokee nation and the first
town Of importance was Talhequah, the
capital, which is situated on the banks Of
the Illinois river, a small, but beautiful
clear stream, which empties into the Ar
kansas twenty miles to the south. The two
nights out before reaching TahleQuah were
without incident, except the visit received
from a band of Indians on the second even
ing from the village of Waululah. The
young ladies had picketed out their horses
cheerful fire, which they had built near the
wagon.


The evening meal had been served and


Miss Stevens was entertaining her compan-
ions by picking Home, Sweet Home" on


the guitar. Music never sounded sweeter
and as the strains were waited down the


stream by which they had camped 1t fell


upon the ears of the drowsy red men at the


village two hundred yards distant. The
daring young heroines were not expecting
a visit from the noble red man, but before


they were aware of IT four big bucks stood
as II thunderstruck within thirty feet Of


the camp drinking In the melody of the


guitar. When the music died away the
Indians simply nodded their approval and
returned to their camp. The presence of

know how badly the young women were
frightened nor how happy they were when

At Tablequah the four young lady adyen-


turers attracted a great deal Of attention.


Here Is the capital of the Cherokee nation,
and here are located all of the leading In
dams OF the tribe. 1t Is the social center Of


the nation, and the young men and women,


half and quarter breeds, whose skin is


whittier than that Of the four sunburned
young women from Arkansas, eyed them


with degree of disgust which was any
thing but pleasant to the travellers. The
campers left Tahlequah the next morning
bright and early, glad to get away from the
peering eyes of Tahlequah's society leaders.


The journey from Tahlequah to Fort Glib


son was made In one day, and the party


went into camp on the banks of the Neosho


river. several miles above. They located in


q grove Of giant trees, where for the first


time during the trip they heard the familiar
MARBLE Of the Arkansas boot owl. In speak


ing of this Miss Myrtle Stanton said she
felt that they were not beyond the borders
of civilization.


For Seven Days.


For seven days the trip continued in a


northwesterly course along the Arkansas
river, where they passed many Indian set
Elements and not a few well-cultivated
farms. In describing this part of the jour-
ney Miss Esterbrook said: ITO the person
who has not visited this country 1 cannot
adequately describe the many changing
scenes to be observed on every side. There
il no section Of the United States so inter-
esting to the lover OF nature. The atmos-
phere in the sunny month of September Is
pure and transparent, and seems to battle
the very heart with gladness. Our journey


was parallel to the Arkansas river for a


distance Of nearly 100 miles. The gigantic
trees. the dense foliage, hanging vines and
sluggish brooks, all indicated quiet. peace
and contentment- Sometimes we scrambled
up broken hills, from the submits of which
we had extended views over wide prairies,
diversified by groves and forests, and on
the other, ranging along line of blue and


shadowy hills to the south, beyond the
waters Of the great Arkansas. Who could
not enjoy such trip?


1--WE were in the region of adventure. and
while many explorers had gone before, and
the once uninhabitable country was now in
the possession of the noble red man, the alb
sence of we'll cultivated farms. towns and
villages invested this part Of the trip with
special interest. The weather was in its
perfection; temperate. genial and enliven-
ing, a deep blue sky, an air pure and bland.
and a beautiful country stretching out far
and wide in the golden sunshine of an
autumn day. An occasional band Of Indians,
now and then a camp of hunters and fishers,


and a world of birds whose plumage and
song attracted and received our complete


admiration. At night when We retired for
rest from the tedious travel OF the day, the
whippoorwills and big boot owls would lull
al their
the morning at first peep Of dawn the mock
ing bird, the blue jay. the wren and the
brown thrush would greet US with their
medley"


None hut brave and resoute women would
have attempted such a trip as this unac-
companied by escorts. But with firm de-
terminate ton to complete the trip and with
confidence in their own courage these dar-

Attack OF French Socialists Upon q Catholic


Meeting.


Socialists at Roubsix. France, yesterday
stormed a hall in which Catholics were having Q
meeting. When the rioters had broken in the
doors several Catholics tried to bar their
progress into the meeting. The rioters threw
them down and forced their way to the platform,
where the priests had raised an altar and placed
a crucifix. They spit on the crucifix, broke it
into fragments and tossed the pieces into the
congregation. The priests, hoping to allay the
excitement, began to intone anthems. Their
calmness only aggravated the ugliness Of the
mob.


The priests were attacked, knocked down,
carried to the doors and thrown into the streets.
While some of the rioters drove out the mon.
women and children Of the congregation, others
smashed the furniture in the hall. Many wo-
men and several men were severely injured by
being knocked down and tramplsd while the
rioters were ejecting them.


The police did not arrive in sufficient force
to control the mob until after the hall had been
emptied Of the Catholics and all the furniture
had been destroyed. Numerous arrests have
been made, and more are expected to follow.

1900 tons of sulphur on board the Brit

vessel with water and scuttle her, but
Professor Price, a chemist who had been
consulted last night, advised different
plan. Four chemical engines were sum-
moned and poured carbonic acid gas
in the hold of the vessel. These
were insufficient, and seven empty
whiskey barrels were charged with
soda, marble dust and sulphuric acid,
and the carbonic acid gas generated
therefrom was turned into the hold. The
experiment was 60 successful that the
chemical engines were this morning
withdrawn, but the improvised fre ex-
tinguishers today continued work. This
evening the decks of the vessel are per-
fectly clear and not sign of fire is seen
anywhere. The damage cannot yet be
estimated.

The feathered tribes have many pecu-
liar ways and farcies about the details
of their toilets. Some birds use water
only, some water and dust, while others
prefer dust and no water. Birds are not
only exceedingly nice in their choice of
bath water, but also very particular
about the quality of their toilet dust. "
Wild ducks, though feeding by salt
water, prefer to battle in fresh water
pools, and will fly long distances inland
to running brooks and ponds, where
they preen and dress their feathers in
the early hours of the morning. Spar
rows battle often, both in water and in
dust. They are not so particular about
the quality of the water as about
the quality of the dust. They prefer
clean water, but have seen them take
dip in shallow pools that were quite
muddy. The city sparrow must take a
water bath where he can get tin the
streets or on the tops of houses but he
is most careful in his choice of his dust
bath. Road dust, the dryest and finest
possible, suits him best. | have noticed
the city sparrow taking his dust bath in
the street, and invariably he chooses a
place where the dust is like powder.
cartridges prefer dry loan. They like
to scratch out the soil from under the
grass and fill their feathers with cool
earth. Most birds are fond of burnt
ashes. Some early morning take a walk
across field that has been burnt over,
and see the number of winged creatures
that rise suddenly from the ash heaps.
A darting form, small cloud of ashes,
and the bathers disappear New York
Home.

Prosecuting Attorney Pugh called Judge
Miller's attention to the case which was brough,
some time ago under the old law charging
James O'Donnell with keeping an unlicensed
bar in December.


Lawyer Daniel E. Cahin appeared for the
defendant, and he raised the point that the
case could not be tried because Of the recen;
act which repealed the old law.


Mr.. Cahill read the repeating clause, as fol-
lows:


THAT this act shall be in lieu Of and as a
substitute for all existing laws and regulations
sale Of distilled and fermented liquors

parts Of laws Inconsistent with this act, excep,
such laws as are applicable to the sale Of liquor
within one mile of the Soldiers Home, be, and
they are hereby, repealed"

maintain charge such as WAS brought against

discussing the matter Judge Miller said
that where the offense charged was alleged

the law the information was proper
and the defendant was properly proceeded
against, but when there is q repeal without a
saving clause the prosecution must necessarily
fall. The judge said he had examined Mary
land authorities and found that they were all

why do women work." asks Walter

VICTORIA, Sept l5.-[Speeial. The
steamers Topeka and Thistle, bringing
the Canadian boundary commission
party from Alaska. arrived this

commissioner. reports that despite the
continuous rains and successive cloudy
days, much more has been accom-
p,ished than was anticipated at
the outset, the Photographic sur
vey system. which was entirely depended
on, proving a complete success. When
the explorers left for north, though
it was August, summer had gone
and winter snow was failing IN
the mountains and operations were
necessarily adjourned till next year.
During the past six months Topographic
cal survey has been made OF the country
from Burrows bay 10 Linn canal. includ-
ing 800 miles of coast line and the coun-
try inland for about thirty miles
The many photographs taken from
mountain tops, with field notes
accompanying, have been carefully
packed and go forward to Ottawa tomor-
row. These photographs will be de-
veloped and the several districts
mapped by the surveyors in charge
of the respective parties. Their
work being connected by King himself
and the completed map SO secured will
subsequently ;, be dovetailed with the
record of the American explorers. All
the territory traversed has been ex-
ceptionally rugged with towering
mountains. great glaciers, tremendous
canyons and rapid rivers. Absolutely no
agricultural land exists in the disputed
strip thus far prospected, nor is the
timber land specially attractive. though
hemlock and FIR of average size are found
on the slopes. Whatever value the conn
try possesses lies in the minerals and it's
four rivers. thelatter teeEaing with salmon
of the same varieties as are already vel.
known to commerce. Game, big and
small, has apparently deserted the land
and no Indians make it their home.


Prof. King and his chiefs of
staff leave for the East to-
morrow aud in October will meet
Prof Mendenhall, the American COM
missioner, when plans for next season will
be matured. The surveys from Linn canal
to Mount st. Elias remain to be completed,

the commissioners will talk much about
the probable outcome of their labors.

gales that swept over the North and Baltic
seas l27 fishermen were drowned Off the

Hartlepool fishing fleet

suffered damage to the extent of f1O0 600.

commons today regarding the loss of life

president of the board of trade, replying

and Irish coasts two hundred and thirty-
seven persons had been lost: The coast
guard life boats had saved five hundred

Washington coast, attended with loss of
life, occurred three miles north of the
Quillayute River early Wednesday morn

paraiso went ashore and was totally
wrecked.


Captain Meyer. his wife and four sea-
men were drowned. The remainder OF
the crew, nine IN number. f1oated ashore
on the wreckage and made their way up
the beach TO Neah Bay. where meager par
ticulars were telegraphed to the Post-ln-
telligencer News Bureau to-day.


The Leanor was caught in a westerly
storm Tuesday night. The captain lost
his bearings and the vessel was driven
ashore on the rocks. As soon as the bark
struck she commenced to break ND.


Captain Meyer caught his wife in his
arms. leaped overheard, and attempted TO
swim ashore. about quarter OF a mile DIS
tant. They both went down.


The bark broke into three pieces, and
four seamen were drowned. The mate
held to piece of the keel for FIVE hours
and finally f1oated ashore. The other eight
seamen reached shore completely ex-
hausted.


The weather was bitter cold. and the
easterly storm drove huge seas over the ill
fated vessel.


Later in the day searching expedition
recovered the body of the captains wife.
The remainder of the crew walked from
QuilIayute River TO Neah Bay and tele-
graphed for assistance. Chilean Consul
Macondray lefs tonight on the tug Discov-
cry for the scene of the wreck.


The bark Leanor sailed from Iquique for
Moodyville to load lumber. Captain Meyer
is an old Pacific Coast navigator, and has
frequently visited Puget Sound in the
Chilean bark Louisa Martha. accompanied
by his wife, whom he married in South
America several wears ago.

| What mighty changes the white man is


making all over the face OF Africa! Mil


lions OF natives feel the impulse. for good


or i'll. Of the strange influence; but they do


not know yet the tremendous consequences
! in which the web Of new conditions will in
| volve them.


| Ten years ago the most dreaded tribe OF
equatorial Africa were the Nasal. Their


home is west and northwest Of Mount


Kilima-N jaro. but their murderous raids
covered vast area from the sea far in
land to the springs that feed Victoria
Nyanza and the Nile. No Swahili trading
caravan. less than thousand strong. dared
venture among them, No missionary risked
his life within their borders. No explorer
fathomed the geographic secrets Of their
land. No cattle-breeding tribe. for hun
dreds Of miles around was safe from their
resstlcss forays; and when JOSEPH THoM-
son at last passed unscathed through Nasal
Land to the great lake. the achievement
Won him enduring fame.


All this is now changed. Even the Swa-
hill porters have lost much Of their terror
before the once dreaded Nasal warrior. Eng
lish fortified posts are planted in his land.
Little missionary bands have safely crossed
the lofty plateau where his women and
children tend their herds. The apparition
OF Ell Moran. in his war plumes. out for q
cattle raid. Is no longer troubling native viii
layers hundreds Of miles from Nasal Land


Capt. PRINGLE Of the Victoria Nyanza
railroad survey tells us that the Nasal are
no longer arrogant in their dealings with
Europeans. They regard the white man
with respect. They ask for presents. but
do not demand tribute. They treat visitors
courteously. do not demand the payment
Of toll from every passing caravan. and
have ceased to force their way into the
white mans tent and order him to take off
his boots and show his toes.


Perhaps their recent misfortunes. not less
than the display Of European power have
modified the arrogance and improved the
behavior OF the Nasal. Once they would
eat nothing but beef or mutton. But
their countless herds have been nearly
annihilated by the cattle plague that has
swept across Africa, and even the warriors
have been compelled to subsist on the de-
spised -four OF the neighboring agricultural
tribes. Scarcity OF food has done something
to lessen their pride and make them more
amenable to reason.


Capt. PRINGLE says the Nasal are now
willing to make treaties with the Europeans
and 1t Is believed they would abide by them.
II they treat them properly. the British
may yet turn the remarkable discipline and
solderly qualities Of this powerful tribe to
good account.

The principal destruction follows: Pitts

ASHLAND. Wis, July 3l.-A crisis was
reached in the lumber-shovers' strike this
morning. The strikers openly defied the
officers of the city and county. closing with
them in hand-to- hand battle. in which
blood was shed freely. The Shores Lum-
Der Company sent word to Mayor O'Keefe
that it had commenced loading boats with
non-union laborers and asked for police
protection. The Mayor sent Chief of
Police Schwarz and some officers to tho
decks, where they we're joined by Sheriff
O'Brien and his deputies.


Work had hardly commenced, however,
when great mob of. strikers swarmed
down. The foremost of them were forci-
bly, handcuffed by the officers and others
were arrested who were afterward res
cued from the police by their fellows. A
desperate hand-to-band contest followed.
The officers were nearly all bruised with
clubs and stones. and non-union men were
struck down with clubs and terribly
beaten. They fled panic-strcken. fol
lowed bv the strikers, and were met by
officers who protected them from further
violence. Forty of the rngleaders among
the strikers have been arrested. Mayor
O'Keefe says that the president of the
Lumber-shovers' Union assured him that
no violence would be committed and he
now swears that the city will protect non-
union labor at any cost.

among the merchants of Panama over the

ships bring American goods and provis-

across the isthmus is $14 per ton, for mer-

rates make the competition between the

road, impossible. Local newspapers de-
nounce the unjust competition. The Star
and Herald says the refusal to grant
through bills of lading and exaction of
local rates on cargoes brought by the
Pacific Mail makes it impossible for the
company to carry freight between New
York and San Francisco. The new COM
pany therefore enjoys q monopoly of the
California trade.

placed in the hands of the United States
Marshal for service.

Flames Destroy the Principal Business


Street of the CITY.


During heavy wind fire broke out at Fargo,
N. D.. yesterday, at 2 p. m, and the whole city
was threatened. The principal business street
of the city lies within the district already
burned and the finest business blocks are in
ashes. Many residences also went down before
the flames.


Most Of the buildings were frame and offered
small resistance before the rush Of flames sent
against them by the gale, that was blowing
thirty miles an hour. 1t was feared the fire
would pass the barrier of the river and destroy
the town of Moorhead. Two thousand people
have been made homeless.


Moorhead people threw open their hotel and
houses for the homeless. The loss cannot be
estimated. 1t is believed that 200 buildings,
large and small. have been burned. The fire
started in sales stable and spread with awful
rapidity.


The fire crossed the river to the Moorhead
side at the Fargo roller mill, which was burned.
Among the principal firms already burned are:
Herman, dry goods: Cranes restaurant. nagill,
farm machinery; Northern Pacific elevator
buildings. Western Union Office, Morton, real
estate: Red River Valley National Bank, Daily
Forum, Merchants State Bank, opera
house, Z. S. Tyler, real estate: John Deer's i'm
PIGMENT house, Coles livery. Wilson'S restau-
rant, Grand Hotel, Flemings drug store, Veder
& Lewis grocery, Christiansons drug store,
sheridan Hotel. Appel Bros, Minneapolis Dry
Goods Company, Logan's studio. Ames iron
works. Centennial House and Vanbrunt imple-
ment warehouse.


The loss is at least $4,000. 600. The bridges
between Moorhead and Fargo have beeh
burned and all Geographic communications are
cut of.


Assistance arrived at the scene from Grand
Forks and Duluth and Crookston was asked for
help.


4, Jas. J. Hill telegraphed from ST. Paul order
ing the immediate opening of the Grand Pacific
Hotel for the use of homeless people in Fargo.

A cable dispatch from the congo, says
the New York Sun, announ ces that the
railroad has been completed from Matadi
to Palaballa. ten miles After the track
layers reached that point mile and half
of the road was completed in ten days.
though nearly two years were taken to
build the first ten miles. The railroad has
been carried beyond the obstacles that long
made rapid progress impossible; and now
the great enterprise will be easily pushed
forward until the upper river. at Stanley
pool, is connected with navigation on the
lower Congo.


Mr.. Stanley said once that all the resour-
ces OF commerce on the upper river would
not be worth copper until better means OF
transportation were provided. This was
possible view, for the traders of England,
Belgium. Holland and France, in fact, have
pushed their enterprises above the contract
region OF the lower river, have established
stations 1906 miles inland, have transported
dozen steamers to Stanley Pool, and thou
sands OF pOrters have been carrying their
merchandise 235 miles around the cataracts.
About 40. 600 carriers in the past two years
have been engaged in the transport service.
La another year or so the railroad will be
completed and then this army OF porters
will have TO seek other employment, for the
railroad will monopoiize the carrying trade.


The merchants of Belgium, however, took
Stanley's words TO heart and a company
called the Society of the Upper Congo, or
gaDiZed 10 develop commerce in the Congo
basin, began TO study the feasibility of
railroad along the 235 miles of Congo
cataracts. Then steamboats, to Stanley
Pool had unimpeded navigation along
tributaries. They desired first TO learn
IL the trade prospects of the Upper
Congo region would justify the heavy cost
of railroad, So they sent an expedition
four years ago, which spent year in
threading the waterways OF the upper
Congo, taking a sort OF census OF the people,
and making a thorough study of the coun-
try. The exploring party then drew up
careful report with regard TO the natives,
their desire for trade, the Kinds OF mer-
chandise they would buy. and the various
products that could be secured for return
eargoes TO Europe.


The company were well pleased with the
report and at once sent out TWO other eXpe-
ditions, one 10 make surveys along the south
bank and the other along the north bank,
to decide the best route for the railroad and
its probable cost. This work occupied an
other year. and after all this preliminary
work it was decided TO build the line on the
south side of the river. starting from Matad,
ninety miles above the ConGo's mouth. The
engineers decided that the line, after skirt
ing the Congo for FIVE miles, should ascend
L
bala. From this point TO Stanley Pool there
are few engineering difficulties. Ii was esti-
lated that the entire cost OF road and equip
ment would be 100000.


The money was raised and the Congo
State gave the company valuable conces-
sious in lands and privileges to help carry
out the enterprise. Agents were sent all
over Africa " hereyer IL was thought natives
could be hired as tTaeklayeTs and laboTers.
European carpenters, biacksmths and
other artisans were sent to the Congo TO
superintend departments and instruct
natives TO carry on various sorts of labor.
Al firt most of the army OF workmen were
secured from Zanzibar, Sierra Leone,
Lagos. Accra aud the Kru coast Of Liberia.
Then the Dshomey, Senegal and the Angola
coasts furnished their contingent, and
finally many workmen were employed from
the lower Congo tribes. Last summer the
fierce OF black laborers numbered 2500, OF
whom 1900 had cCme from various points on
the Guinea coast.


Then came busy days at Matadi. The
place was An arid. rocky, uniDvitiDg spot
and only two buildings and ten Europeans
were there two years ago this month. One
of our pictures shows part of the town as
il appeared last spring, including the
hotel and the galyanized-iron buildings Of
the Congo State. To-day the town con-
tains about 800 Europeans, fifty
more than Stanley left behind him





to Eurcre after founding his stations
About 1000 native employees OF the railroad
are also quartered at Matadl Three thou
sand people live in and around the little
town. The white population includes Bel
gians, English, Portuguese, Italians.
FreuchmeD, Dutch, Germans. Swedes and
Greeks, and besides the employees OF the
railroad and the State there are quite
number of traders and missionaries.


Harder reilroad building is rarely seen
than that which ushered in the beginning
of the enterprise. One picture shows the
first few miles Of the road along the side OF
Matadi Hill. The arrow on the right shows
the situation of.Matadi. The river here flows
swiftly and is full Of eddies and whirlpools.
A little further up the river are the Yellala
Falls, and the scene of this picture Is where
fuckers Inflated expedition, In 1916, first
heard the roar If the great cataract and
found, in few weeks crowded with dis
aster that those falls formed n barrier they
could not pass. The depression in the big
hills at the left OF the picture Is the Leopold
Ravine, up which the railroad turns TO reach
the heights of oalab8la.


The road. from the starting point at
Matadi, all along this hill slope, and up the
rayine TO Palapalia has been blasted out of
solid quariZtte OF extreme hardness, and
progress has been made with the utmost
difficulty. The slope along the river is very
PERCEPTIONS, and in many places the track
bias been laid between TWO solid walls of
rock. which were blasted foot by foot. Still
greater difficulties were encountered IN the
ravine, up which tie roadbed had 10 be
made at q steep gradient until 1t reached a
height of about 1000 feet above the river.
The work is carried on under the direction
of Captain 1hys, who has been in the SER
vice of the Congo Stale and the Society Of
the Upper Congo for years.


Another picture shows the bridge. about
200 feet long, that has been thrown over the
raw
is the largest bridge Yet put in place along
the line. The able young engineer who
built it. Mr.. jean Baptiste Glaesner. wrote
10 his friends two months ago, Next week
l shall complete the bridge. and then shall
come home TO rest" The poor fellow had
oyertaxed his strength. and the next
steamer from the Congo bore the sad news
that poor Giaesner was dead and the friend
who sent the tidngs enclosed photograph
of The mpleted bridge. to which the young
man had devoted MT nths of hard work that
cost him his life. Seven bridges of i'm
pOrtance must he built before The line
reaches Stanley Pool. The longest, over the
Ngongo River. will be $50 feet long


One problem which gave the engineers
some trouble was how 10 dispose of the tor
rents of water which would be sure to pour
down over the track during the heavy trOp-
zeal rains. 1t was feared that incessant
trouble during half the year would be en-
countered from this source. An effective
solution OF the problem seems 10 have been
reached. At all places where large torrents
occur steel aqueducts are building that will
carry the floods down the hills and under
the railroad track.


At first the company had considerable
difficulty in scouting enough provisions for
its army Of w0rkmen, as it was very costly
to bring provisions from up the river. The
coast regions far and wide were levied upon
for supplies. The workmen have been
we'll fed on rice, corned beef, dried fish,
vegetables and biscuits; and now that the
road is pushing along the plateau 1t Is ex-
pected that provisions will be more easily
obtained and at cheaper rates. Seven loco
motives and thirty cars are on the track,
and large part of them have been kept
busy carrying railroad material and pro-
visions as the road advanced.

PANAMA, April 4.-News of the signal
defeat Of the Government troops near
Iegucigalpa. Honduras, was received in
this city late last night by mail. This re port
was confirmed in advees brought later by
the officers of the steamer Barra-
couta, who added the information
that the revolutionists had finally
triumphed and that Polcarpo BOnla
had been proclaimed Provisional President
of the Republic. The news reached here
from Managua. Nicaragua. which is tho
hotbed OF sympathizers with the revclu-
tionists and it is therefore given with all
due reserve


General Terrencio Sierra led the advance
upon the Government position. His troops
pushed forward with great bravery, hut
their assault was resisted with courage and
determination equal to their own. aud for
more than two hours the battle ragged with
out apparent advantage on either side.


Then the revolutionists decided upon a
bolder and more decisive move. Their
lines seemed to waver for moment and
then they dashed forward in solid ranks.
They fell upon the Government army with
terrific force and battered it in a murdeTous
fashion. General VasQu,z's troops resisted
the onslaught with great valor, and
for few moments it seemed as
though they could beat back the
attacking columns, but the reserves
were brought forward, and the dash against
the Government troops became hotter than
before. Tie revolutionary troops broke
through the Government lines in the GEN.
Ter, cutting the defending army into two
forces and spreading Generalization and
terror among the troops. From that moment
the battle was won for Bonilla's army.


The revolutionary loss was great. and
General Sierra Bonllas, chief of staff. was
himself badly wounded. BOnillas' victor
ious soldiers slaughtered the fugitives
without mercy and scores are reported to
have been killed while fleeing for safety.


General Vasquez himself fled toward Vii
lanera, leaving Bonilia a clear road on
which to march to Tcgucigalpi. 1t is said
that many Government soldiers who es-
capped from Bonillas' troops went through
the Los Angeles Valley, where they COM
mitted many atrocities.


After the great victory Bonllla marched
at the head of his victorious army into
Tegucigalpa. lie was received with en-
thusiasm, and without opposition was pro-
claimed Provision President of the republic
He accepted the Office and at once took
charge of the Government.


Later reports say that General Vasquez
has been captured by the reYoutionists.

GREENOCK, Scotland, Feb. 1.-THE Allan
line steamer P0meranian, from Glasgow
for New I 0rk, returned here to-day after a
frlgatful experience. When about 1900
miles out. during heavy storm, everything
above decks was swept away by a huge
wave. which boarded the vessel when no.
body was prepared for it. John Cook and
John Hamilton, second and fourth officers;
James Pritchard and Fred Westbury, stew
ards; Peter Mclean and William Urquhart,
seamen; James and Lillian Gibson, Jane
Caftsry and Johu Stewart, first cabin. and
David Forbes, second cabin. were washed
overheard and drowned. Captain Dalziel
was dashed against the bulwarks and so
severely hurt that he died next day. The
vessel then put about and started back under
command Of the first officer.


The Pomeranlan encountered boister0us
weather Immediately after leaving port. 1t
was thought the wind would soon blow itself
out, but instead OF abating the gale in
creased in severity until the day Of the dis
sster and the 4h of February dawned with
a frightful gale raging and tremendously
high sea running. The matches were bat
tened down aud covered with tarpaulin S,
the yentilators turned to leeward and every
precaution dictated by good seamanship
had been taken to prevent the water get
ting below. Several heavy seas were
shipped, but they did no damage.


Suddenly a tremendous sea reared its
crest short distance ahead Of the steamer
as she plunged down the wave and before
she could rise the sea came over the star
board bow and tons of green water swept
aft Almost at the same time the fall
ing wave astern came aboard. The
result almost deies description. The deck
saloon, chart house, bridge and boats were
smashed to pieces and partly washed over
bOaId. the deck was covered with an almost
inextricable mass Of wreckage and the ut
most confusion regned.


At first the full extent Of the disaster
was not known. The steamer began 10 pay
off before the wi nd and sea. and it was at
once seen that the quartermasters had been
carried overheard. Two sailors sprang to
the wheel and soon put the steamer on her
course, and then it was found that Captain
Dalziel was missing. He was last seen
standing on the lee side Of the steamer aft
OF the saloon in conversation with a saloon
passenger named John Stewart They
were both dashed against the deckhouse
and then carried with terrific force and
jammed beneath the after steam winches.
Captain Da!ziePs legs were broken and he
sustained internal injuries. He was care
fully removed to his room, but he died the
next morning. Stewards legs were also
broken, and he sustained other injuries,
from the effects Of which he died in few
hours.


At the time of the accident Second Off
Ger John Cook was standing on the bridge
with John Hamilton. the fourth officer, and
L =" :. them we're carried overheard and
drowned.


In the saloon deckhouse when the sea
broke over the steamer were James Gibson
and Lillian Gibson Of Dalketh and Jane
Caffery Of Londonderry, all cabin passen-
gers. They were carried over the side and
not afterward seen. David Forbes of Dun
dee. second cabin passenger. and James
Pritchard and Fred Westbury, stewards,
were also lost in the same manner.


When the sea boarded the steamer every
man about the deck who saw 1t coming
grabbed hold OF the stanchions or OF any,
thing else convenient, and it is due to this
fact that the loss Of life was not much
larger. For the time the utmost consterna-
tion prevailed, but this gave way to feel
ing of sadness when it was found that so
many lives had been lost.


With Captain DalZel fatally injured and
unconscious in his cabin, the command OF
the steamer devolved upon the first officer.
When the chartro0m was carried away the
charts. sextants, quadrants and, in fact.
everything essential TO the navigation of
the ship. went with 1t. The binnacle- box
and the compass On the bridge had also
gone overheard, and had it not been that the
after compass remained ii is doubtful If the
steamer would have reached port for many
days yet.


The situation Of affairs was terrible. The
first officer called the remaining officers of
the steamer into consultation, and it was
decided to put about and return to Green
ock This was at once done, and without
any instruments with which to take observa-
tions the voyage had to be made entirely by
dead reckoning and was necessarily slow.
The first officer is highly commended for his
sklllfuI seamanShip In navigating the Pom
eranian under such adverse circumstances.


The scene at the burial Of Captain Dal-
Ziel was one of the saddest ever witnessed
at sea. The crew and passengers stood
silently weeping. During the simple and
mournful ceremony the waves were running
mountain high and all felt that they too
might soon be with the departed captain.


Veteran sailors who were on board the
ship declare that during an experience of
thirty years the storm was the worst they
ever encountered. If the ship had not been
stanch and discipline good they would have
fouDdered. Although the discomfort en-
dured was very great, nobody complained.
but every body looked forward with eager
ness to n safe arrival on land. and all were
too glad to be alive TO complain Of lack Of
accommodations.


The interior of the Pomeranian was
badly damaged and will require extensive
repairs.

Shortly after O'Clock this afternoon Solo

of age. and living at 915 9Th street northwest

was drowned.


He accompanied by young friend and
they arrived at the beach about 10 o'clock.
The ice. which is only four inches thick was
quite rotten. but Notwithstanding this about
100 boys we're enjoying the sport. Young
Cohen and his friend were more
daring than the rest and skated far out to
where large barge, about 600 feet from the
shore, lay frozen in.


THE ICE BROKE AND HE WENT UNDER.


While skating around the barge young Cohen
led the way. Suddenly he broke through the
ice and disappeared. His friend hastened to
his assistance, but he, too. broke through. He
managed, however. to drag himself out, but
Cohen slipped under the ice and was seen
no more.


In q moment the cry "Boy drowned" rang
out and the ice was cleared of skaters. The
Waterman ran to the nearest telephone and
sent word to the police boat.


While they were waiting for the relief
policeman arrived. but he seemed in daze and
allowed a score more of small boys to walk
out to the place where the accident occurred.


Up to the time The STAR went to press the
body had not been discovered.

of Swarts Luis-on- -Overyssel held an out
door meeting today. After listening to

rioting. They visited all the finest
houses, smashing windows, and stoned

stones. A rioter was shot dead by the

carbine. Two policemen were

rioters were wounded. About

took place at Pekila and Sappermeer.

in Sappermeer after six policemen were
wounded. The military were called out
and charged the mob, They were re-
pulsed, leaving behind soldier, who
was almost beaten to death. They then
opened fire. Two rioters were killed,
five seriously and many slightly
wounded. Twenty men were arrested.

Old Robert Schmidt, who had passed for
many long years in California as Herman
Weber, was buried yesterday in Odd Fell
lows Cemetery. while his two widows
wept over him.


The scene at the grave was pathetic.
At one side little group of mourners
stood apart. The central figure was Mrs.
Weber, whom Schmidt married under that
assumed name. Opposite them across the
grave were the dead mans widow, Mrs.
Schmidt, her daughter and grandchildren,
The two women whom Schmidt had
wronged gazed at different places On his
coffin lid, while a number of men wearing
badges of benevolent societies were grouped
between.


Sehmidt's or Weber's funeral Che was
buried under the assumed name) arrived
at the cemetery after 3 o'clock in the after
noon. There was only one carriage be-
hind the hearse. but al the gate this
modest cortege was met bv members of
Apollo Lodge No. %, /. o. o. f., and of
the Verein Eintrachf, who escorted II TO
the grave. The carriage contained Mrs.
Weber-widow No. 2-and her friends.
But Mrs. Schmidt was not there.


When Mrs. Weber stepped from the car
riage she was dressed in the deepest
mourning and heavy veil over her face.
She walked behind the coffin, leaning on
friends arm, and stood beside the grave
while the burial service of the odd Fell
lows was read. Her sobs were painful to
hear, and told more than words how deep
was her affection. Once she became al
most hysterical. pointing toward her hus-
bands first widow and endeavoring to get
away from those around her. They led
her back TO the carriage which waited close
by.


Where the other bereaved woman came
from nobody present seemed to know, be-
cause when Weber's remains were carried
down narrow avenue she came from be-
hind a pile of boxes and stood of modestly
from the grave. She wore no widows
weeds; no black veil. She was plainly
and quietly attired in black. Mrs. Schmidt
did not give expression to her grief,
although she felt as keenly as the other
woman, wept bitterly.


Long before the earth was filed in over
the coffin Mrs. Weber drove away. But
Mrs. Schmidt remained until the workmen
formed a mound and placed board st the
head. 1t was then that the widows tender
feelings showed themselves. With her
daughter she placed three bouquets on the
grave and knelt down to pray.


The dead man married Mrs. Schmidt in
Wisconsin thirty years ago. After the
war he deserted her at st. Louis and came
to California. where he married again
under the name of Herman Weber. His
first wife found him here and then Weber
solved the difficult problem surrounding
him by jumping into the bay.

est confusion took place inside

who committed suicide was the the one
that stepped In between Mr. and Mrs.
Sapp.


Maud Shoudell was formerly of Pitts
burg, Tenn. where her husband ran a
hotel. She left him and after
coming here was a waitress in res

Mrs. Cleveland left this morning for he
summer home, Gray Gables, Buzzard's Bay
Massach usetts. The President did not accom-
pany her, as he found it impossible, with thu
press of official duties, to commence his vaca
tion at this time. but, as announced in TIL
STAR last week, hopes to join his family before
the 4th Of July, and to spend most of thai
month and August with them.


The train upon which Mrs. Cleveland was
passenger was the regular Pennsylvania 9:4(
express for New York. She travelled in Vice
President Thomson's private car, and it was the
last in the makeup of the train. 1t was ready
for her occupation far in advance of the rest Of
the train, but she did not reach the Baltimore
and Potomac depot until 9:35, and consequently
walked through the station to the train, just as
did the couple of hundred other people who
were to take the train.


Mrs. Cleveland hurried across the platform
through another gate, near the one through
which the rest OF her fellow travellers had to
stop and show their tickets, and was aboard her
car before scarcely any one had recognized her
except the train officials who were on hand to
bid her welcome.


BABY RUTH AND HER ATTENDANTS.


With Mrs. Cleveland were Nurse Annie and
Baby Ruth. Aboard the car Mrs. Cleveland re.
treated from observation and busted herself
with getting settled for her long ride. The
nurse and Baby Ruth had the drawing room,
with its big observation windows, all to them
selves as the train pulled out Of the station.


Mrs. Cleveland's travelling dress was a new
dark blue serge. made with full skirt. A shirt
waist OF white lawn, dotted with blue, a blue
ribbon belt with fancy buckle, and q dark
blue straw hat. trimmed with blue ribbons and
dark blue quilts, were the finishing touches.
She carried jacket to match her skirt


Baby Ruth had one Of her simplest white
muslin frocks on and white lace cap. She
looks little thin and delicate and not near so
rosy she did month ago. The warm
weather has not agreed with her very well. and
hence Mrs Cleveland's g anxiety to get her of to
a cooler climate.


Mrs. Cleveland took six or seven servants
with her. The men. headed by the White
House steward, ST. Clair. had their arms full OF
small chairs. push wagons and other parapher-
MALTA, representing Miss Ruth Cleveland
dreams of happiness when the winds blow over
the rock-bound coast of Buzzard's Bay-big
bugs and little ones, baskets and hampers. and
an immense variety OF other articles. Two OF
the maids escorted good-sized black shaggy
dog. to whose collar strong chain WAS fas-
tened.


EXPECTED BACK IN SEPTEMBER.


1t is understood that Mrs. Cleveland will re-
turn here early in September. Her mother,
Mrs. Perrine, will soon make her visit at GRAY
Gables, and it is not unlikely that some Of the
cabinet members and their wives will visit
there also after the President gets there for his
summer outing.

Experiments with Dried Brewers Grains


as Food for Horses.


Some interesting feeding experiments
the New Jersey Agricultural Experiment
Station by Acting Director James Nelson,
Prof. Edward b. Voorhees, and Louis A.
Voorhees, The experiments were to COM
pare the results of feeding dried brewers
grains and oats. The experiments proved.
it is said, that the brewers grains furnish
more economical food with equally sat-
isfactory results The dried grains were
cheaper pound for pound than the oats,
and being richer In the valuable nutrients,
proteine and fat permitted OF a
material reduction In the cost of the
ration. Tho work performed by
the horses was quite as great and their
health and vigor quite as good as when
oats constituted the main part of the ra
tion. Horses on the New Brunswick City
Railroad were chosen as the subjects of the
experiments. Eight horses we're taken.
Four were fed ration of hay wheat bran,
corn and brewers grains while oats were
substituted for the dried grains with the
four others, the tosal weight Of each set
differing only by ten pounds. The expert
ment continued for three months, At the
end Of that period the average increase in
weight of the horses fed with eight pounds
of brewers grains per day was forty five
pounds per horse, while with like quan-
tity OF oats, it was 81 pounds per horse.

Mississippi Valley.


CHICAGO. March pa special to the Herald
from Memphis SAYS:


The damage done by Thursdays cyclone in
the Mississippi valley is enormous While the
loss OF life is not as great at first reported
the damage TO property will reach q 1000 oO0
The telegraph wires are still demoralized and
reports are coming in slowly from the storm
districts and il will be several DAYS before the
full extent OF the disaster will be known


THE DEATH LIST.


The death list foots up eighteen, while the list
Of injured viii run up into the hundreds. The
names Of the dead at Kelly, Miss. 90 far as
known are:


Harriet Smith. Mary Williams, Susan WILL
iams and two unknown negro men.


The dead elsewhere are: Richard Heard,
Shubuta. Miss; John Heard, Shubuta. Miss
Eli Prince. Elizaville. Miss; Drury Su merars
family Of nine, Shaws, Miss.


The names OF the injured at Kelly, 90 far as
known, are follows: Richard Pine wife and
children. all badly injured by the collapse OF
their house; one OF the children will
head and shoulders; may die. Chris Burfurd,
internally injured; will probably die. Mrs.
Sarah Hart, two ribs broken and internally in
lured; may die. Marion Mason, cut about the
head. Mrs: Mason, badly hurt about the hips.
Harriet Prince. badly injured George Berry
and his wife, badly injured. Gus Bills, right
eve knocked out E. H. Mclaughlin, shoulder
broken. Wiley Mclaughlin. arm disiocated
The injured at other points: s. K. Davis,
Charlottesville, Ark Fourteen negro tenants,
jured. Jim Carroll. Spring Greek, Tenn,
fatally injured. Aleck Poisons. Spring
Creek, Tenn. struck by timber and
seriously injured. Twenty-one school children
more or less seriously injured. The majority of
the killed and injured are negroes.
THE PATH OF THE CYCLONE
The first heard of the cyclone was in north
Louisiana and southern Arkansas. 1t crossed
the Mississippi few miles above Greenville,
devastating plantations. wrecking farm houses
and uprooting grand forest trees. The path of
the storm was about half mile wide and moth
ing was left standing in its track.


The first fatality occurred near Shaw 6 station.
Miss. where the house of Drury Sumeral. a
prosperous and industrious colored farmer
was leveled to the ground. killing the entire
family of nine persons. The cyclone passed
through the suburbs of Shaw's and demolished
several residences and small stores, but no one
was killed.


The hurricane then changed its course
slightly and travelled the right Of way OF the
Yazoo and Mississippi Valley railroad until it
entered Cleveland. Miss. where q public school
building, several houses and stores were RACED
to the ground. No fatalities occurred at Cleve-
land, but several people were struck by flying
timbers and more or less injured.
NEARLY EVERY BUILDING WRECKED.
Leaving Cleveland the cyclone passed within
mile of Clarksdale, town Of 1000 inhabi-
tants, and next struck Tunica, the county
seat Of Tunica county. Nearly every build
ing in the place was wrecked The newly
erected court house went down before the wind 9
fury. The colored school building was wrecked
and over thirty children MANNED. As the cy-
clone left Tunica it divided. one portion travel
ing in northeasterly direction, while the other
took a northwesterly course and again crossed
the Mississippi river into Arkansas, where il
spread ruin through three counties.
GREAT DAMAGE AT KELLY.
The towns Of Charlottesville and Vincent
were nearly wiped of the face Of the earth, and
the storm then took q northeasteriy course,
reaching Kelly, Miss, about 4 O'Clock in
the afternoon. There the greatest damage
was done. Six persons were killed out
right and scores injured. Not q building was
left standing, the fragments being strewn over
the country for miles. The damage to property
in the vicinity Of Kelly will reach $50 600.
After leaving Kelly the cyclone passed into Ten
nessee, the next place to fall in its path being
Spring Greek, q small town in Madison county,
where several people were injured, but no one


Immense damage was done in Sumner
county. At the Kennesaw breeding farm the
roof Of the large two-story residence was
blown off, the large brood-mare barn
demolished and a fine race mare belonging
to Louis Emmon of Illinois killed and several
others belonging to Mrs. James Franklin
fatally injured. The large stock barn OF Harry
Shaffer was blown down and one horse killed.
All over the county barns. outhouses. fences
and trees were wrecked. The damage cannot
yet be ascertained.


dispatch from GAINESVILLE says that many
residences and business houses were unroofed
by the wind in that city and much damage done
by the rain. In Montgomery county many
head Of stock were killed, barns destroyed and
great damage done.


The railroad depot at Oak Grove was COM
pletly destroyed. No lives were lost.

Cmbria Broken.


Upon the arrival at Hamburg Yesterday
Of the Hamburg American Line steamer
Bohemia interviews were had with several
persons aboard of her in regard to her
attempt to tow the disabled Cunard liner I'm
bria. and to the report that the towing hawser
had been cut on board the Bohemia.


Everybody on board the steamer emphaticallv
denied that the hawscr was cut. They say that
the weather was fairly calm when the steel
hawser and several other lines from the Bohe-
mia were made fast on board the Umbria
The Bohemia then forged ahead with the
Cunard liner in tow, but in the evening vio-
lent storm set in. Both vessels pitched heavily,
and the strain upon the towing lines was tre-
mendous. At 10 o'clock at night it was snow
ing heavily, and at that hour the starboard line
and the port hawser parted.


The breaks were not close inboard but a con-
siderable distance from the Bohemia. MANY
feet Of hawser were left trailing astern when
the break occurred, and this fact effectually
disprovcs the statement that the hawser was
cut on board the Bohemia When the lines
parted the Bohemia stopped and sgnaled re-
peatedly to the Umbria, but no answer was
received. When daylight broke the sea was
closely scanned for the Umbris. but no sign of
the Umbria could be seen. The Bohemia there
fore proceeded on her voyage. The crew OF the
Bohemia knew that if they succeeded in taking
the Umbria into Halifax they would receive a
share Of the salvage money, and they were en-
thusiastic ut the prospect When the lines
broke they were greatly disappointed, as their
hope of reward disappeared.


According to those interviewed the COM
mander Of the Bohemia would have been only
| too glad to have towed the Umbria into port
and had his lines not broken he would have
certainly done SO. The breaking of the lines
was due to the great strain upon them and not
to their being cut on the Bohemia, and any
statement to the contrary is not based upon
knowledge Of the facts.

With the tertiary age, or the age of

Corydon, Ind, Aug. Z. - Last night
Boone township; this county, was made
the scene of the most terrible shooting
affair that ever occurred in this part of
the state. A large crowd of men went
to the house of William and Ed Conrad
for the purpose of lynching the two boys,
who were suspected, of killing their father
last winter. The young Conrads had
received notice some time ago that if
they did not leave the neighborhood they
would be lynched. Upon this notice the
boys armed themselves with shotguns and
revolvers and awaited their coming. The
boys secreted themselves outside their
house when the crowd approached and
fired into them, killing John Timberlake
and William Wiseman, after which the
crowd dispersed, and before they could
command themselves they were again
fired into and Edward Houston and
Isaac Howe were instantly killed and
William May was fatally shot The
mob comprised about 100 men, and those
killed and wounded are the best in the
township. The two Conrads escaped.
Intense excitement prevails throughout
the southern part of the county. The
Conrad boys have always been regarded
as vicious and worthless.
