WASHINGTON, Jan. 3.-Weather crop
bulletin: While the deficiency in tenn
perature for the month of December was
greatest in the northwest, the cold was
relatively more severe throughout the
southern states. The cold wave ex-
tended southwark, causing killing irosts
as far south as Jupiter. Fla, and alon
the gulf coast, on the 29th, and for sew
eral days the temperature was from 10
to 20 degrees below freezing over the
greater portion of the southern states.
Excessive rains occurred in the
lower Mississippi valley, and generally
over the regions south of Missouri and
north OF the Rio Grande valleys. The
month was generally dry throughout
the regions on the Atlantic coast, and
over the Ohio valley and the lake re-
gion. On the Pacific coast, while the
rainfall was generally less than usual, it
was timely and sufficient in quantity
to prove of benefit to the farmers. The
month closed with the ground covered
with snow from New York and the
upper Ohio valley westward to the
Rocky mountains, and the ground bare
over the greater portion of Missouri,
Illinois and Indiana, and thence south
ward, thus leaving over half OF the
winter wheat without the protection
afforded bv snow.

The Northern Pacific Railroad Company
received lot of engines in 1890 with
62-inch driving wheels and cylinders 19x24
inches. The wheels of these engines are
being changed 10 81 inches and the cylin-
ders to 1915 inches, with the same stroke.
The cylinders were made originally thick
enough to stand reboring. This change
has given the engines greater capacity,
and twenty-four cars can now be hauled
on divisions where eighteen was the Limits
before


This is an interesting evidence of the
fact that in some cases locomotives have
been built with too small cylinders. Evil
dence has been coming in during the past
two years that when the reduction in CYL
inder volume was made in locomotives in
this country about five years ago. it was
carried too far by some. and it has been
found that the single expansion iocomo-
tives which have the largest cylinders
make the best showing in competition
with compounds. Probably this results
from the greater expansion obtained with
the larger cylinders.


1t has become quite evident from certain
notable cases that the size of the cylinders
is not entirely independent of the work to
be done. and locomotives working on
heavy grades should have considerably
larger cylinders than engines Of the Same
weight used on comparatively level track.

PITTSBURGH. Sept 11.-There was riot last
night at Beading. q small coal mining station
on the Pittsburgh. CHARTERS and Youghiogheny
Railroad. some thirteen miles from here.
About $50 striking Italian miners. armed with
shotRuns and revolvers and pieces OF iron.
marched down the main street shooting and
shouting.


William and Thomas Beading. who own the
mines. aided by six OF their English miners,
were armed with rifles and revolvers. Others
volunteered their services to protect life and
property. but the Beadlings sent them away.
thinking fewer men more likely to avert q con-
fiict All night the eight men were besieged
IN the company's storehouse The guns OF
the strikers flashed from the hill across the
railroad. from the windows Of the coal tipple.
and from the houses Of the Italian miners.
The mob stood on the hillside above the works
firing. yelling. and throwing pieces Of iron.
Bullets and missiles whizzed over and against
the storehouse and building. Windows were
broken, and much damage DONE but no one
was shot.


At daylight Beadlngs' band charged out
upon the Italians. who scattered and fed. after
few parting shots. Then Mr.. Beading went
to Mansfield. Ave miles below. and swore out
warrants for the arrest OF about thirty Of tho
mob for riot and disorderly assemblage. Con-
stables Strengthen berger Foster and Bell
reinforced by English miners, arrested
twenty eight OF the Italians Three Of
the ringleaders were captured in their
homes. Twenty were captured only after
a chase OF several miles. The Ital-
ians' houses were searched and fifteen
guns mostly shotGuns. and some revolvers
we're secured. The most OF the Italians had
fed to the hills. Those captured were taken
to Mansfield for safekeeping and hearing.


William Beading said to-day:


I've could have shot those Italians down
like dogs. but We held our fire. and events
proved that We acted wisely. Despite the
threats OF the Italians we worked up to the
usual time Saturday afternoon. We would
have started this morning. but it might have
led to bloodshed. We intend to start to-mor-
row morning."


The trouble arose over a misunderstanding
about pay. Recently. owing to tho financial
stringency. the BeadinG Bros. had to pass a
pay day. They asked the men to wait until
Sept %. promising to pay In full then. The
Italians demanded their pay at once and quit
work, but did not take away their tools. They
were told that they must work under the ar
rangement agreed upon or get out. About 300
men are usually employed in these mines. Of
whom over 200 are Italians.

Harris wanted them. They reported that

gaze, not uttering word when the YER
dict was announced. Mrs. Evans accom-
panied her husband to the jail. but just "a
she entered the Jail door she tainted and

an hour.

distance from the buildings. At the same time

nue sprang great masses of flame which flooded

however. detracted somewhat from the effect.

Nine years ago Capt HOLM spent months
In the most northern settlements OF the
isolated east Greenland Esl,imos. For gen.
erations they had been cut off from the
rest OF the world until year or two before
HOLM aud his party made their advent
The Danish explorer told the natives many
things about the world that astonished
them greatly. and he whetted their curos-
ity to learn more. About year lator small
bands OF these natives. who mum bored. &C.
cording to HoLM's census. 41s persons,
made their appearance around the southern
end OF Greenland. and told the people of
Julianehaab and other west coast settle
ments that they had come to stay. Their
experience with white men had pleased
them. They had heard that white men
lived on the west coast. and that others
visited that part OF Greenland every year.
They said they wished to live, hereafter,
where they might meet white men and
trade with them.


Last year Lieut.. RYDER. another Danish
explorer. visited the settlements OF these
Angmagsalik natives where HOLM had dis
covered them. He found only 22l people.
where HOLM had counted 4l9 souls. The
mortality among them had been very
heavy. but emigration was chiefly respon-
sibe for the fact that the population had
been reduced nearly one-half.


A curious fact about these Esklmos was
illustrated by the difficulty RYDER expert
enced in his efforts to learn how many of
them had died since HOLM lived among
them. They can hardly be induced to speak
of their friends who have died. They ex-
poet the dlrest evils will befall them IL they
mention the names OF the dead. and this
superstition. more potent among them than
In any other branch Of the Ee kimo family.
has had noteworthy influence upon their
language.


Philologlsts have thought it not little
remarkable that the Eskimo dialects.
spoken by widely separated branches of the
family differ SO little ono from another.
From Alaska to Labrador and Greenland
these few thousands of people, living along
coast fringe of enormous length, divided
into groups by uninhabited districts thew
may not have crossed for generations. all
speak, practically, the same language.

BUFFALO, NY, July 19-The excursion
train carrying the Sunday schools of Bethany
and Bethlehem churches of Buffalo, on the
Western New York and Pennsylvania railroad,
was wrecked at East Aurora at 7:45 O'Clock last

teen or moro others, old and young, more or

facilities the full details Of the wreck were not
obtaiuable until after midnight


The accident ia one Of the most remarkable
in the history Of railroad wrecks Two engines
were crushed in masses Of twisted steel and
lying in the bottom of the turntable, with
timbers. broken glass and iron Of the first two
coaches.


These coaches were filled with excursionists,
and that they escaped with no more serious in
Jury il almost miraculous.


As near can be learned the accident was
due to carelessness.


The evening local train from Buffalo to East

locomotive to the turntable preparatory to
heading 1t toward the city for the morning trip.
The switch was left open, as the engineer in
tended taking his engine out on the main track
and back to the siding for the night. Just be-
yond the turntable is q sharp curve and beyond
that the track rises in heavy grade.

saw the danger, but it was too late to stop his

Rine already upon the table. The baggage car

wreck.

understandable, the women and children being
thrown under and over the seats and through
the windows. cut with flying splinters, broken
limbed and bruised. Then the cars took fire

fire department

There one act that came very near being

pose but after that was done he fell fainting

afterward.

Harry Sauer, both legs broken. The splin-
tered bone broke through the flesh and it was

Arthur Sauer. leg broken and seriously

Take large white or yellow freestone
peaches. They must not be too ripe.
Scald them with boiling water cover
and let stand until the water becomes
cold. Repeat this scalding. then take
them out, lay thin on soft cloth.
cover them over with another cloth, and
let them remain until perfectly dry.
Now put them in stone jars and cover
with brandy. Tie paper over the tops
of the jars and let them remain in this
way one week. Then make a syrup,
allowing one pound of granulated sugar
and half-pint of water to each pound
of peaches. Boil and skim the syrup,
then put in the peache and simmer
until tender then take the peaches out.
drain and put them in glass jars. Stand
the syrup aside to cool. When cold, mix
equal quantities of this syrup and the
brandy in which you had the peaches.
Pour this over the peaches and seal.

being one OF the best shots In Skagit county.
On Tuesday morning, with his dogs and rife,
Smith started out to hunt for deer. His hounds
were nervous and restless and led him for some
distance The rev snow had obliterated the
deer tracks, but he could tell from the way the
hounds were behaving that there was game
somewhere. Suddenly the dogs started forward
on jump, and In about . second there was
great commotion; there were sounds Of break
ing brush. followed BY snarls, growls and ear.
piercing screams. Then Eve frantic cougars.
followed by the yelping hounds, bounded into
view not forty rods from the spot where the
hunter stood with rife In hand. He instantly
drew . bead on the foremost cougar and fred.

trembling to the ground-dsad. The dogs freed

got away.

Newport Daily bews. She was comfortably
placed in the big chair and was enjoying the
first sensation OF breathing IN the fumes. There
was delicious murmuring that reminded her
Of the sounds Of . lovely summer day, bees
humming and all nature At lullaby. But she
was still conscious, just dazed enough to fancy
that long time was passing and she
was consuming quantities of gas with
out its having the desired effect. She
must be taking more than the doctor could
afford to give her. Several times he had
lifted her fingers to see If they were limp, and
now he suggested that she keep her hand as
long as possible held up from the wrist.
Madame had tender heart, and in her half
asleep state 1t overpowered her head. The
DENTS. could never waste on one patient that
amount of gns. 1t was her duty to deceive him
and stop this great drain on his pocket. So
she let the hand fall limp and played insensi-
BILE. Out came one tooth with horrible
wrench that invaded every fiber Of her being
and brought her back to her full senses with a
bound. The doctor was amazed. and both were
amused when the state of the case WAS realized.

NEw YORK. April 26.-The phantom ships
which sailed in out OF the nlists Of the sea yes-
terday were bright and majestic realities IN the
glorious sunshine this morning. The
only element wanting TO insure the triumph
ant spectacular success OF the great
naval parade was supplied by the perfect
weather. Not trace WAS left OF the
steel gray clouds and rain and fog OF Yesterday.
Clear skies, bright sunlight and brscing brcezes
gave q setting to . panoramic scene whose
beauty and suggestiveness have never been sur
passed.


In the sharp. clear light Of the early morning
every distinctive feature OF the great warships
stood out in bold relief. Anchored in two great
columns stretched over the whole surface OF
the bay, the vessels Of each Of the ten uationali
ties represented could be distinguished at .
glance.


The snow-white hulks and graceful outlines
Of the American feet were not more conspicu-
Gus than the huge black hulk Of the British
flagship, the towering military masts Of tho
French Jean Bart, Of the sharp lines
of the crack German cruiser Kaiserin
Augusta with her formidable Krupp guns. Of
set by the squat outlines of the Dutch VanSpeyk.
which again contrssted with the graceful build
Of the swift Argentine Nuevo de Julio, and the
massive armament of the Brazilian battle ship
Aquidaban.


EARLY MORNING SILENCE


The most striking feature of the scene was
the absolute silence that prevailed during the
early hours Of the day. Each of the formid-
able death-dealing engines Of destruction
lay motionless at anchor. reflected in the
placid waters of the bay by the early
morning rays Of the sun like the often quoted
Painted ship upon painted ocean" There
was grim suggestiveness of represented force
and stern discipline in this impressive quiet.


But it did not last long. As the morning
wore on and the preparations for breaking
anchor began the scene changed TO one Of
brisk animation and life. The bay became
alive with pleasure craft OF every description,
and the patrol boats had difficult
task to keep the anchorage grounds clear Of in-
truders and 10 permit the formation Of the
columns in which in stately procession the ves-
sells were to pass through the Narrows into the
upper bay and to move up the Hudson river
to their assigned stations, and there to await
tomorrow's review.


THE FORMATION OF PARADE


1t was shortly after o'clock when Admiral
Gherardi's flagship gave the preliminary signal
to break anchor and fall into line. The start
ing side, or right-hsnd column, looking toward
the bows Of the vessels, commanded by the
British admiral, Sir John Hopkins, consisted OF
foreign vessels In this order:


British-Blske, Australia, Magicienns and
Tartar.


Russian-Dimitri Donskoi, General Admiral
and Rynda-


French-Arethuse, Hustard and Jean Bart.


1taly-Etna, Giovanni aud Bausan.


spain-Infanta Isabel, Reins Regents and


Brazil-AquidAban, Tradentss and Repub-
lica.


The port or left-hand column, commanded
by Admiral Gherardi, consisted Of the Ameri-
can feet, with some of the visitors thrown
into balance. in the following order:


American-Philadelphi Newark. Atlanta,
San Francisco, Bancroft, Bennington, Bslti-
more. Chicago, YORKTOWN. Charleston, Eesuvius
and Concord.


Argentine De Julio.


Holand-Van Speyk.


Germau-Kaiserin Augusta and sesadler,
with the American monitor Minatonomoh
bringing up the rear.


PROMPT START


The start WAS made SO promptly at 945 that
thousands Of spectators who had gathered to
witness the spectacle from the Navesink high
lands and the heights Of Fort Wadsworth
and other points Of vantage on Staten
Island had hardly taken up position
before the guns of Forts Hamilton and Wads-
worth doomed their welcome to the advancing
feet. Steaming neck and neck the two sd-
mirals and their hagships led the way at Q rate
Of between eight aud nine knots al hour.


A brisk breeze curled the waters into white
caps breakers. but the magnificent ships glided
along so smoothly that their motions scarcely
seemed perceptible A cable and half length
600 yards) separated each ship from the other,
and this distance was maintained with absolute
precision.


CONTRAST BETWEEN AMERICAN AND FOREIGNER.


The contrast presented by the snow-white
American feet and the dark-hulled foreigner
was very perceptible they moved along side
by SIDE each heightening the effect of the other.
The two schools Of naval architecture (for
nearly all the ships in the fleet not
American built were Of English construction)
were strongly marked and every patriot felt
within glow Of pride that the new navy Of the
United States did not suffer by the COM
parison-


The time occupied in passing the forts was
exactly half an hour.


The naval ships, after passing the Narrows,
entered the upper bay. and the feet Of excur-
sion steamers and yachts and Big boats fell
in and became volunteer escort. The
scene then became OF combined
grace, animation and beauty never 10 be for
gotten. The absence of cannonading left the

derbilt, where they stopped for few
moments and watched the stonecarvers at
work on the new addition to the building

passed them. little dreaming that the
pretty, golden-haired woman in the sailor
hat, whom they almost brushed against
was Princess of Spain.

Fifty-eighth street, and slowly sauntered
toward Sixth avenue, engaged in animated
laughing heartily at some sally Of the
Prince. They paused for a while, and
watched the trains on the Sixth-avenue
Elevated Railroad. Then they continued
their walk to Seventh avenue. turned and
walked up to Fifty-ninth street.


There they crossed over to the park side
and stood for some time viewing the
Columbus monument. They then turned
about and slowly sauniered along the
Fifty-ninth street park front and returned
to the hotel after an absence of an hour
and quarter. Davis was considerably
disturbed until lie found they had re-

Women turned away, unable to stand the

hardened men of the sea which did not

Everything possible was done for the
sufferers. and with good medical attend
ance, plenty OF wholesome food and warm
clothing they were soon revived sufficiently
to tell their story.


Captain Drummond's boat was amply
provlsioned, but on March 81, at o'clock,
the wind blew into a sQuall and raised
fearful, choppy sea. The boat was headed
toward the gale and an endeavor made to
keep her bow on to the seas.


just few seconds before the boat was
capsized William Drummond. son of the
captain and second mate of the King
James, called out to the men to swing her

The crew obeyed with alacrity, but the

could not be brought about in time


On, on came the great wave, a monster
wall OF green water. 1t caught the tiny
fabric and Tor moment 1t seemed that she
would ride the sea in safety, when with
hiss and roar the roller combed over at
the crest. broke and filed the boat with

Peter Petersen and William Balze, sailors.

upturned boat, then thrown back within

succeeded in catching hold at the bow and
chung on with the rest of the crew for three
hours before the boat could be righted
This was done with difficulty and when
accomplished II was discovered that all the
provisions had fallen out.


For twelve hours the boat was full of
water most OF the time. Seas continually
broke over 1t, and most of the men were so
overcome with exposure and exhaustion
that they lay down in the bottom of the
boat with nothing but their head, arms and
shoulders out Of the water. In this posi-
ton one man died and his body was con-
signed to the waves.


The third day part OF the water was
balled out. The weather had moderated,
and an occasional sunbeam found its way
through the clouds and impaired little
warmth.


Too latel Hunger. cold and thirst had
begun work long hours before. Two more
men died and third had but a short while
TO live. The remaining men raved, cursed
and beat the water with their hands, i'm plor-
ing heaven to end their existence. Those
who remained rational were afraid to sleep
lest their insane shpmates might kill them.


The fourth day came and still no sail in

and during the day two more, including
Third Mate Drummond, the captains son.
He raised himself on his elbow and tried 10
call to his father, fell back and expired
with moan.


Captain Drummond laid his head upon his
dead sons breast and sobbed pitifully. The
remaining survivors could scarcely gather
strength enough 10 throw the bodies over
board, but finally succeeded in doing so.


Another day of agony. during which
Flint and Sperry were In sem!-conscious
condition, and the following morning the
Los Angeles was sighted.


Captain Drummond raised himself with
the greatest exertion, signaled frantically to
the steamer, then dropped, more dead than
alive, in the bottom of the boat.


The names of the men who died are:
William Drummond. third mate; Oliver
Robinson, John johnson, William Spence.
Peter Petersen, John Williams, William
BalZe. Second Mate David Ireland, John
Chrisly, Stephen Breeder. Frank Kenyon
and Henry Bruce.


Before the boat was capsized one of the
men wanted to land on an island which was
sighted.


The gale sprang up shortly after he was
put ashore, and the boat could not 60 near
enough 70 get him off again.


The officers OF the Los Angeles say that
Captain DrummOnd is inclined to blame the
first mate as being the cause of disaster
among the men of the unlucky boat, claim
ing that the mate dIs0beyed orders in not
keeping within sight. and instead sailed
away on his own course

Barbara. The surviving crew has been paid

HARRISBURG, Pa. May 2.-The train bearing
President Cleveland on his return to Washing
ton from Chicago passed here at els o'clock
this afternoon.


The train arrived in Pittsburg at 7:40 o'clock
this morning, ten minutes behind time. There
were very few persons about the station and
the only persons visible on the train were the
porters and trainmen. The President and all
the members of the party we're still sleeping
when the train pulled out for the east at ESQ.
having stopped just long enough to change en-
gines.


The trip from Chicago to Pittsburg was made
without incident. At all stations between
Chicago and Fort Wayne crowds assembled to
see President Cleveland, but he was very much
fatigued and remained in his car. Shortly
after leaving Fort Wayne he retired for the
night.


Several hundred people had assembled at
the station here. and cheered the President and
Secretary Carlisle when they appeared on the
platform of the train. Speaker Thompson in
troduced all the members of the legislature
who could get near the President, and many
others shook his hand.

The famous women warriors Of Dahomey,
who have fought SO desperately against the
French troops, are trained for service with q
severity beside which the discipline of our
soldiers is luxurious ease. They are recruited
from girls Of thirteen or fourteen years and
also from the ranks Of criminals and evildoers,
for any crime is pardoned to the woman who
enlists among the Amazons. They are COM
PEELED to sleep outdoors in all kinds Of weather.
to suffer blows and kicks without complaint and
are often kept starving for days. For the pur-
pose Of acquiring proficiency in scaling walls
the scantily clothed warriors are compelled to
Chamber to the top Of walls thickly covered with
thorny cact, the ground beneath being strewn
with broken glass. Before going into battle
liberal quantities o. rum are given to them to
give them the daring recklessness which marks
their attacks. They fire rapidly for little
time then, charge upon the enemy with their
knives, and even when shot down viii fight to
the last breath, stabbing blindly at their assail-
ants and biting and tearing at their legs when
they can no longer stand.

The famous women warriors of Dahomey,
who have fought so desperately against the
French troops, are trained for service with
severity beside " hich the discipline of our
soldiers is luxurious ease. They are re-
cTuited from girls of 10 and IA years, and
also from the ranks of criminal and evil
doors. for any crime is pardoned to the
woman who enlists among the Amazons.

without complaint, and are often kept starv-
Ing for days. For the pupose of acquiring
proficiency in scaling walls. the scantily
clothed warriors are compelled 10 clam her
to the top of walls thickly covered with
thorny cacti, the ground beneath being
strewn with broken glass. Before going
into battle liberal quantities of rum are
given to them TO give them the daring reck-
lessness which marks their attacks. They
ire rapidly for little time, then charge
upon the enemy with their knives, and even
when shot down will fight to the last
